lead: This unit is about the bottom layer of a network: how bits actually leave one machine and arrive at another as voltages, light pulses or radio waves. After it you can compute a channel's maximum bit rate, pick a cable or antenna for a job, draw the waveform that carries any bit stream, and size a shared link.
about: Unit 2 covers the physical layer from the signal upwards. Chapter 2.1 describes analog and digital signals and how sampling converts one into the other. Chapter 2.2 shows the three ways a signal is spoiled on a link, and 2.3 turns those ideas into the two hard limits on bit rate, Nyquist and Shannon. Chapter 2.4 chooses the physical path: twisted pair, coaxial cable, fibre or free space. Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 put data onto that path, first as line-code voltages, then riding a modulated carrier. Chapter 2.7 shares one link among many users with FDM, TDM and WDM, and 2.8 spreads a signal over a wide band so it survives interference and eavesdropping. Every chapter carries worked numbers, because exams here ask for arithmetic, not definitions.

chapters.idea: A signal carries information as a changing physical quantity: smoothly in analog form, in fixed steps in digital form, and three numbers — amplitude, frequency and phase — describe it.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as its own chapter; most fold it into the first lecture. Define signal, periodic signal, amplitude (volts), period T (seconds), frequency f = 1/T (hertz), phase (degrees or radians) and wavelength λ = v/f (metres, v = speed in the medium). Show one sine wave and one square wave side by side. For digital signals define level, bit interval, bit rate (bit/s) and the difference between bit rate and baud rate, plus baseband versus passband. Close with the sampling theorem as a statement only: a signal whose highest frequency is f<sub>max</sub> is fully described by samples taken at f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>max</sub>; then three lines on PCM — sample, quantise, encode — so that 8000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 kbit/s for voice makes sense.

figure.aria: One sine wave of period 4 ms drawn above a two-level digital square wave that changes level every 1 ms.

chapters.example: An analog signal completes 50 full cycles in 0.2 s and travels in a cable at 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Find its frequency, its period and its wavelength. A digital signal then sends 1000 bits in 0.25 ms; find its bit rate and bit interval. Frequency f = 50 ÷ 0.2 s = 250 Hz, so T = 1/250 = 4 ms and λ = (2 × 10⁸) ÷ 250 = 800 km. Bit rate = 1000 ÷ (0.25 × 10⁻³ s) = 4 × 10⁶ bit/s = 4 Mbit/s, and bit interval = 0.25 µs.
chapters.trap: Mixing up bit rate and baud rate, and putting milliseconds into f = 1/T without converting to seconds; a signal with T = 4 ms is 250 Hz, not 4 Hz.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, for where the physical layer sits under the data link layer.
chapters.leave: Line codes to 2.5, carrier modulation to 2.6, and the full PCM quantisation-noise derivation to a signals course.

chapters.idea: A signal loses its identity on a link in three separate ways: it gets weaker, its shape smears, and unwanted energy joins it.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities treat impairments as a chapter of their own. Attenuation: define decibel for power, dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁), and for voltage, dB = 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁); negative dB means loss; dBm as power relative to 1 mW; state that loss in a cable grows with distance and with frequency. Distortion: different frequencies travel at different speeds, so a composite signal's components arrive out of step and adjacent bits overlap — name intersymbol interference and say equalisation (a filter that compensates) fixes it in one line. Noise: thermal noise (power = 4kTBR, k = Boltzmann constant, T = kelvin, B = Hz, R = ohms), induced noise, crosstalk, impulse noise; then signal-to-noise ratio S/N as a power ratio and SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log₁₀(S/N).

figure.aria: The signal power falls from 10 mW to about 0.3 mW over 5 km while the noise power stays flat at 0.02 mW.

chapters.example: A 10 mW signal enters a 5 km cable whose loss is 3 dB per km. Find the output power, and the SNR in dB if the noise at the output is 20 µW. Total loss = 3 × 5 = 15 dB, so P₂ = 10 mW ÷ 10^1.5 = 10 ÷ 31.6 = 0.316 mW. Noise is 0.02 mW, so S/N = 0.316 ÷ 0.02 = 15.8, and SNR = 10 log₁₀(15.8) ≈ 12 dB.
chapters.trap: Using 10 log₁₀ for a voltage ratio (it must be 20 log₁₀), and dropping the minus sign and then reporting a loss as a gain.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for signal power, frequency and the sine wave.
chapters.leave: Equaliser design and filter theory to a signals course; error detection and retransmission that hide the damage to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Two formulas give the ceiling on bit rate: Nyquist for a noiseless channel and Shannon for a real, noisy one.
chapters.depth: Nyquist bit rate = 2 × B × log₂ L, where B is bandwidth in hertz and L is the number of signal levels; explain that 2B comes from the sampling theorem, so it is a sampling argument, not a law of nature. Shannon capacity C = B log₂(1 + S/N), with S/N a power ratio, not dB; show the conversion SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log₁₀(S/N) both ways. Show that the largest number of levels that still reaches the Shannon limit is L = √(1 + S/N), so the two formulas agree when the constellation is chosen properly. Work log₂ by hand (log₂ X = log₁₀ X ÷ 0.301). Contrast: more bandwidth always helps, more levels only helps until noise wins — quote the voice-band modem that stalled near 35 kbit/s.

figure.aria: Two rising straight lines: the eight-level Nyquist rate is 6 kbit/s per kHz, the 35 dB Shannon capacity is about 11.6 kbit/s per kHz.

chapters.example: A telephone channel has B = 3 kHz and SNR = 35 dB. Find the Shannon capacity, then the Nyquist rate for 8 signal levels. SNR = 10^3.5 = 3162, so C = 3000 × log₂(3163) = 3000 × 11.63 ≈ 34.9 kbit/s. Nyquist with L = 8 gives 2 × 3000 × log₂ 8 = 2 × 3000 × 3 = 18 kbit/s. The channel could carry about 35 kbit/s, so with only 8 levels the Nyquist limit is the one that binds; to reach 35 kbit/s the modem needs L ≈ √(3163) ≈ 56 levels.
chapters.trap: Putting the decibel figure straight into Shannon's formula; 35 dB is a ratio of 3162, and S/N must be that ratio.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for bandwidth and frequency, 2.2 for what S/N means.
chapters.leave: Modulation schemes that use L levels to 2.6; information-theoretic proofs to a later course; error rates to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The path between sender and receiver is either a solid conductor or glass (guided) or air and vacuum (unguided), and bandwidth, loss and cost decide which one a link uses.
chapters.depth: Guided: twisted pair — UTP and STP, categories Cat 3 to Cat 6, RJ-45 connector, 100 m limit, cheap, used from telephone pairs to Ethernet; coaxial cable — 50 Ω baseband and 75 Ω broadband, TV and cable internet, better shielding than twisted pair; optical fibre — core, cladding, refraction and total internal reflection, critical angle, step index versus graded index, single mode versus multimode, LED versus laser source, SC/ST connectors, splicing, huge bandwidth, no crosstalk, no EMI, so Indian backbones and FTTH use it. Unguided: radio waves, terrestrial and satellite microwave, infrared; ground, sky and line-of-sight propagation; antenna height and curvature of the earth in one line. End with a comparison table of cost, bandwidth, distance and noise immunity.

figure.aria: A two-branch tree splitting transmission media into guided types, twisted pair, coaxial and fibre, and unguided types, radio, microwave and infrared.

chapters.example: A step-index fibre has core refractive index 1.50 and cladding index 1.48. Find the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, the numerical aperture and the acceptance angle. Critical angle θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(1.48/1.50) = sin⁻¹(0.9867) ≈ 80.6°. NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √(2.25 − 2.1904) = √0.0596 = 0.244. Acceptance angle = sin⁻¹(0.244) ≈ 14.1°, so light entering within a cone of about 28° total is guided.
chapters.trap: Swapping the acceptance angle and the critical angle; the critical angle is measured inside the fibre at the boundary, the acceptance angle outside the fibre at the face.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for wavelength and frequency, 2.2 for attenuation in dB.
chapters.leave: Ethernet cable categories as a standard to Unit 3, 802.11 radio details to Unit 3, switching fabrics to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Line coding maps a stream of bits onto voltages or light levels so that the receiver can both read the bits and stay in step with the sender's clock.
chapters.depth: Define signal element, data rate (bit/s), signal or baud rate, and r = data rate ÷ signal rate. Name baseline wandering, DC component and self-synchronisation as the three problems every code fights. Schemes: unipolar NRZ; polar NRZ-L, NRZ-I, RZ; Manchester and differential Manchester; bipolar AMI and pseudoternary; multilevel 2B1Q; block coding 4B/5B and 8B/10B in one line each; scrambling B8ZS and HDB3 with the substitution rules worked on a bit string. Give approximate bandwidths: NRZ needs about N/2 Hz, Manchester about N Hz. Mention that a code must always be quoted with its convention, since Manchester has two.

figure.aria: Two level traces for the bit stream 1 0 1 1 0 0 1: NRZ-L follows the bits, NRZ-I inverts only at each 1.

chapters.example: Encode the bit stream 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 in NRZ-L (1 = high, 0 = low), NRZ-I (invert at each 1, starting high), Manchester (1 = low-to-high, 0 = high-to-low) and AMI (first 1 positive). NRZ-L: + − + + − − +. NRZ-I: − − + − − − +. Manchester, written as half-bit pairs: −+ +− −+ −+ +− +− −+. AMI: + 0 − + 0 0 −.
chapters.trap: Inverting AMI at a 0 instead of at each 1, and forgetting to state which Manchester convention is being used so the answer looks wrong.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for bit interval and levels, 2.3 for why bandwidth matters.
chapters.leave: Framing, bit stuffing and error detection to Unit 3; 4B/5B inside Fast Ethernet to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Modulation moves a signal onto a carrier frequency so it can cross a band-pass channel, and the same three carrier parameters serve analog data (AM, FM, PM) and digital bits (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM).
chapters.depth: Why modulate: antenna size, band-pass channels, frequency reuse, multiplexing. AM: s(t) = A<sub>c</sub>[1 + μ cos(2πf<sub>m</sub>t)] cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), where A<sub>c</sub> is carrier amplitude, f<sub>m</sub> the message frequency, f<sub>c</sub> the carrier, μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub> the modulation index; sidebands at f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>, bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub>, overmodulation when μ > 1; DSB and single-sideband suppressed carrier in one line each. FM and PM: frequency deviation Δf, modulation index β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>, Carson's rule B ≈ 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>), noise immunity versus bandwidth. Digital: ASK and OOK, FSK and BFSK, PSK with BPSK and QPSK (2 bits per symbol), QAM-16 and QAM-64 with log₂ M bits per symbol and a constellation sketch; baud rate × bits per symbol = bit rate. End with the modem as the box that does this at both ends.

figure.title: A modem link
figure.aria: A one-way chain: bits, line coder, modulator multiplying by the carrier, channel, demodulator, bits out.

chapters.example: A 1 kHz tone with peak amplitude 6 V amplitude-modulates a 100 kHz carrier of peak amplitude 10 V. Find the modulation index, the sideband frequencies, the bandwidth and the peak amplitude of the AM wave. Then a QAM-16 modem runs at 2400 baud; find its bit rate. μ = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6, that is 60%, so no overmodulation. Sidebands at 100 − 1 = 99 kHz and 100 + 1 = 101 kHz, bandwidth 2 kHz. Peak amplitude = 10(1 + 0.6) = 16 V. QAM-16 carries log₂ 16 = 4 bits per symbol, so bit rate = 2400 × 4 = 9600 bit/s.
chapters.trap: Reading μ > 1 as deeper modulation: past 100% the envelope crosses over and the recovered audio is inverted and distorted. Second trap: multiplying baud rate by the number of levels instead of by log₂ of the number of levels.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for frequency and phase, 2.3 for bandwidth, 2.4 for what a band-pass medium does.
chapters.leave: Sampling and PCM detail to 2.1; combining many carriers to 2.7; QAM as used in Wi-Fi and LTE to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Many signals share one high-capacity link either by splitting the frequency band (FDM, WDM) or by taking turns in time (TDM).
chapters.depth: FDM: each user gets a band, with guard bands between them, all users transmit at once; total bandwidth = sum of channel bandwidths plus guard bands; examples are radio and TV broadcast and the analog telephone hierarchy. TDM: synchronous TDM with fixed slots, a frame that repeats, one framing bit, and bit stuffing when input rates differ; statistical (asynchronous) TDM where slots are given on demand and each slot carries an address, trading overhead for efficiency. WDM: the same idea as FDM but with wavelengths and a prism, DWDM with many closely spaced wavelengths in one fibre. Give the digital telephone numbers: a T-1 frame is 24 × 8 + 1 = 193 bits at 8000 frames/s = 1.544 Mbit/s; an E-1 frame is 32 × 8 = 256 bits at 8000 frames/s = 2.048 Mbit/s with 30 voice channels and 2 signalling channels. Compare the three in a table.

figure.aria: Two TDM frames of three one-microsecond slots each: user A takes the first slot of every frame, B the second, C the third.

chapters.example: Twenty-four voice channels, each sampled 8000 times a second with 8 bits per sample, are multiplexed with one framing bit per frame. Find the frame size, frame rate and line bit rate. Then find the bandwidth needed for four FDM channels of 4 kHz with 1 kHz guard bands between them. Frame = 24 × 8 + 1 = 193 bits, frame rate = 8000 frames/s, bit rate = 193 × 8000 = 1 544 000 bit/s = 1.544 Mbit/s. FDM: 4 × 4 kHz = 16 kHz of channels plus 3 guard bands of 1 kHz = 19 kHz.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the framing bit, and multiplying the frame size by the bit rate instead of by the frame rate; 193 × 8000, not 193 × 8.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for bandwidth, 2.6 for the carriers that FDM stacks, 2.1 for sampling rates.
chapters.leave: Circuit switching versus packet switching to Unit 1; OFDMA in Wi-Fi and LTE, and CDMA, to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Spread spectrum deliberately widens a narrowband signal over a much wider band using a code the receiver knows, so it survives interference, hides below the noise and resists interception.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Two families. FHSS: the carrier hops among a set of frequencies on a schedule; define hop, dwell time, hop set, slow hopping (several bits per hop) and fast hopping (several hops per bit); one line on Bluetooth using it. DSSS: each data bit is replaced by a chip sequence, typically the 11-chip Barker code, the spread signal is modulated, and the receiver multiplies by the same code to collapse it back; processing gain = 10 log₁₀(chip rate ÷ data rate). State that total power does not rise — the power per hertz falls, which is why the signal can sit under the noise floor — and that the spreading code is what separates users in CDMA. Uses: GPS, Wi-Fi, military links, and interference rejection in a crowded band.

figure.title: Direct-sequence spread spectrum
figure.aria: A chain in which data is multiplied by a pseudo-random code, modulated, sent through a noisy channel, and multiplied again by the same code to recover the data.

chapters.example: A DSSS system sends data at 1 Mbit/s and spreads it with an 11-chip code, giving 11 Mchip/s. Find the processing gain in dB. A frequency-hopping system uses 50 hop frequencies and hops 200 times a second; how long does each hop last? Processing gain = 10 log₁₀(11 000 000 ÷ 1 000 000) = 10 log₁₀ 11 ≈ 10.4 dB, so an interferer must be about 11 times stronger than the signal to break it. Dwell time = 1 ÷ 200 = 5 ms per hop.
chapters.trap: Thinking spreading increases transmitted power or data rate; the power is fixed and the data rate is the same, only the occupied bandwidth grows and the power per hertz drops. Second trap: confusing chip rate with bit rate.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for Shannon and S/N, 2.6 for carrier modulation, 2.7 for sharing a band.
chapters.leave: CDMA as a multiple-access protocol to Unit 3, and spreading codes in GPS and 5G to later reading.
